question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ compute $P(X=5),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\frac{{2}^{x}{e}^{-2}}{x!}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =f(5) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{5}{e}^{-2}}{5!} \\  & ≈0.0361.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Given X∼Po(2), compute P(X=5), rounded to 4 decimal places.

a
0.1115
b
0.1014
c
0.0361
d
0.0802
e
0.0842
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X∼Po(λ), then X has the following probability mass function:

f(x)=λxe−λx!

Here, X∼Po(2), so the distribution of X in this case is

f(x)=2xe−2x!.

Therefore,

P(X=5)=f(5)=25e−25!≈0.0361.

EXPLANATION

If X∼Po(λ), then X has the following probability mass function:

f(x)=λxe−λx!

f(x)=2xe−2x!.

Therefore,

P(X=5)=f(5)=25e−25!≈0.0361.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ compute $P(X=3),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\frac{{2}^{x}{e}^{-2}}{x!}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =f(3) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{3}{e}^{-2}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.1804.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ compute $P(X=3),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\frac{{2}^{x}{e}^{-2}}{x!}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =f(3) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{3}{e}^{-2}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.1804.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Computing a Probability at a Point
question.problem: Given $X \sim \textrm{Po}(4),$ compute $P(X = 2),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
If $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) =
\dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}
$$

Here, $X \sim \textrm{Po}(4),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x) = 
\dfrac{4^x e^{-4}}{x!}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =f(2) \\  & =\frac{{4}^{2}{e}^{-4}}{2!} \\  & ≈0.1465.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{3x}{5}=\frac{6}{5}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3x}{5} & =\frac{6}{5} \\ (-5)\cdot (\frac{3x}{-5}) & =(-5)\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ (\cancel{-5})\cdot (\frac{3x}{\cancel{-5}}) & =(\cancel{5})\cdot \frac{-6}{\cancel{5}} \\ 3x & =-6 \\ (\frac{1}{3})\cdot (3x) & =(\frac{1}{3})\cdot (-6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) & =-\frac{6}{3} \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}

Solve the equation −53x=56.

a
56
b
12
c
13
d
−3
e
−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

−3x5=65

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

−3x5=65(−5)⋅(3x−5)=(−5)⋅65(−5)⋅(3x−5)=(5)⋅−653x=−6(13)⋅(3x)=(13)⋅(−6)(13)⋅(3x)=−63x=−2

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{3x}{5}=\frac{6}{5}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3x}{5} & =\frac{6}{5} \\ (-5)\cdot (\frac{3x}{-5}) & =(-5)\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ (\cancel{-5})\cdot (\frac{3x}{\cancel{-5}}) & =(\cancel{5})\cdot \frac{-6}{\cancel{5}} \\ 3x & =-6 \\ (\frac{1}{3})\cdot (3x) & =(\frac{1}{3})\cdot (-6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) & =-\frac{6}{3} \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{4}=\frac{2}{1}
$$

$$
\frac{x}{4}=2.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4} & =2 \\ 4\cdot \frac{x}{4} & =4\cdot 2 \\ \cancel{4}\cdot \frac{x}{\cancel{4}} & =8 \\ x & =8\end{aligned}
$$

b
53
c
13
d
35

EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

54=3x4

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

54=3x44⋅54=4⋅3x44⋅54=4⋅3x45=3x(13)⋅5=(13)⋅(3x)53=13⋅(3x)53=x

We conclude that the solution is x=53.

c
−2
d
−3
e

EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

−3x2=92

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

−3x2=92(−2)⋅(3x−2)=(−2)⋅92(−2)⋅(3x−2)=2⋅−923x=−9(13)⋅(3x)=(13)(−9)(13)⋅(3x)=−93x=−3

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{3x}{2}=\frac{9}{2}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3x}{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ (-2)\cdot (\frac{3x}{-2}) & =(-2)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ \cancel{(-2)}\cdot (\frac{3x}{\cancel{-2}}) & =\cancel{2}\cdot \frac{-9}{\cancel{2}} \\ 3x & =-9 \\ (\frac{1}{3})\cdot (3x) & =(\frac{1}{3})(-9) \\ \cancel{(\frac{1}{3})}\cdot (\cancel{3}x) & =-\frac{9}{3} \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Solve the equation −23x=29.

a
13
b
5
c
−2
d
−3
e
53
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

−3x2=92

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

−3x2=92(−2)⋅(3x−2)=(−2)⋅92(−2)⋅(3x−2)=2⋅−923x=−9(13)⋅(3x)=(13)(−9)(13)⋅(3x)=−93x=−3

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{5}{2}=\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} & =\frac{x}{4} \\ 4\cdot \frac{5}{2} & =4\cdot \frac{x}{4} \\ \frac{20}{2} & =\cancel{4}\cdot \frac{x}{\cancel{4}} \\ 10 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=10.$

b

c
20
d
10

4
Submit

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

52=x4

$$

$$
\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

$$

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial in One Denominator
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)\cdot (\frac{x-2}{2}) & =2\cdot (\frac{1}{4}) \\ (\cancel{2})\cdot (\frac{x-2}{\cancel{2}}) & =\frac{2}{4} \\ x-2 & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x-2+2 & =\frac{1}{2}+2 \\ x & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Solve the equation 2x−2=4.

a
53
b
12
c
13
d
25
e
52
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=2 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x−22=14

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

(2)⋅(x−22)=2⋅(14)(2)⋅(x−22)=24x−2=12x−2+2=12+2x=52

question.html:
Question 6
?

Solve the equation 2x−2=4.

a
53
b
12
c
13
d
25
e
52
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=2 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x−22=14

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

(2)⋅(x−22)=2⋅(14)(2)⋅(x−22)=24x−2=12x−2+2=12+2x=52

question.name: Question 7
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{2}=\frac{4}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
\frac{x+5}{2}=4
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot (\frac{x+5}{2}) & =2\cdot 4 \\ \cancel{2}\cdot (\frac{x+5}{\cancel{2}}) & =8 \\ x+5 & =8 \\ x+5-5 & =8-5 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Solve the equation 2x+5=14.

a
3
b
−2
c
2
d
4
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=−5 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x+52=41

The above equation simplifies to

x+52=4

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

2⋅(x+52)=2⋅42⋅(x+52)=8x+5=8x+5−5=8−5x=3

Question 7

Solve the equation 2x+5=14.

a
3
b
−2
c
2
d
4
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=−5 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x+52=41

The above equation simplifies to

x+52=4

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

2⋅(x+52)=2⋅42⋅(x+52)=8x+5=8x+5−5=8−5x=3

question.name: Question 8
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=-3$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2}=\frac{x+3}{7}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition and the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{x+3}{7} \\ 7\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) & =7\cdot (\frac{x+3}{7}) \\ \frac{7}{2} & =\cancel{7}\cdot (\frac{x+3}{\cancel{7}}) \\ \frac{7}{2} & =x+3 \\ \frac{7}{2}-3 & =x+3-3 \\ \frac{1}{2} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=\frac{1}{2}.$

last_observation.name: Question 8
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial in One Denominator
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=-3$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2}=\frac{x+3}{7}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition and the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{x+3}{7} \\ 7\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) & =7\cdot (\frac{x+3}{7}) \\ \frac{7}{2} & =\cancel{7}\cdot (\frac{x+3}{\cancel{7}}) \\ \frac{7}{2} & =x+3 \\ \frac{7}{2}-3 & =x+3-3 \\ \frac{1}{2} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=\frac{1}{2}.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Solve the equation 2=7x+3.

a
−32
b
12
c
−3
d
2
e
13
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=−3 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

12=x+37

We can now solve this equation using the addition and the multiplication principle:

12=x+377⋅(12)=7⋅(x+37)72=7⋅(x+37)72=x+372−3=x+3−312=x

We conclude that the solution is x=12.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial in One Denominator
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=7$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{6}{1}=\frac{x-7}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
-6=x-7
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =x-7 \\ -6+7 & =x-7+7 \\ 1 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=1.$

a

1

−1

−2
e

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=7 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

−61=x−71

The above equation simplifies to

−6=x−7

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

−6=x−7−6+7=x−7+71=x

We conclude that the solution is x=1.

question.name: Question 11
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+2}{6}=\frac{x}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $6.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{x+2}{6}=\frac{2x}{6}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot \frac{x+2}{6} & =6\cdot \frac{2x}{6} \\ x+2 & =2x \\ 2 & =2x-x \\ 2 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=2.$

Question 11
?

Solve the equation 6x+2=3x.

a
13
b
16
c
−2
d
2
e
−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=−2 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x+26=x3

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator 6. The above equation becomes x+26=2x6.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 6⋅x+26=6⋅2x6x+2=2x2=2x−x2=x

We conclude that the solution is x=2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+2}{6}=\frac{x}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $6.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{x+2}{6}=\frac{2x}{6}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot \frac{x+2}{6} & =6\cdot \frac{2x}{6} \\ x+2 & =2x \\ 2 & =2x-x \\ 2 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=2.$

Question 11
?

Solve the equation 6x+2=3x.

a
13
b
16
c
−2
d
2
e
−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=−2 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x+26=x3

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator 6. The above equation becomes x+26=2x6.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 6⋅x+26=6⋅2x6x+2=2x2=2x−x2=x

We conclude that the solution is x=2.

question.name: Question 12
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Solve the equation 23x+2=−4x.

a
−47
b
32
c
37
d
74
e
−12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=−23 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

3x+22=−x4

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator 4, as follows:

6x+44=−x4

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 4⋅6x+44=4⋅(−x4)6x+4=−x6x+x=−4x=−47

solution.reasoning: With x\ne0,-\frac{2}{3}, cross-multiplication gives 2x=-4(3x+2), hence 14x=-8 and x=-\frac{4}{7}, option a. Substitution makes both sides equal 7. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=\frac{1}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x}{3}=\frac{3x-1}{9}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $9.$ The above equation becomes

$$
-\frac{3x}{9}=\frac{3x-1}{9}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9)\cdot \frac{3x}{-9} & =(-9)\cdot \frac{3x-1}{9} \\ 3x & =(-1)\cdot (3x-1) \\ 3x & =1-3x \\ 3x+3x & =1-3x+3x \\ 6x & =1 \\ (\frac{1}{6})\cdot 6x & =(\frac{1}{6})\cdot 1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x-5}{6}=\frac{x}{2}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $6.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{x-5}{6}=\frac{3x}{6}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot \frac{x-5}{6} & =6\cdot \frac{3x}{6} \\ x-5 & =3x \\ x-x-5 & =3x-x \\ -5 & =2x \\ (\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-5) & =(\frac{1}{2})\cdot (2x) \\ -\frac{5}{2} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2}.$

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial and a Monomial in Denominators
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x-5}{6}=\frac{x}{2}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $6.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{x-5}{6}=\frac{3x}{6}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot \frac{x-5}{6} & =6\cdot \frac{3x}{6} \\ x-5 & =3x \\ x-x-5 & =3x-x \\ -5 & =2x \\ (\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-5) & =(\frac{1}{2})\cdot (2x) \\ -\frac{5}{2} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2}.$

Question 14
?

Solve the equation 6x−5=2x.

a
65
b
13
c
−5
d
−52
e
25
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=5 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x−56=x2

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator 6. The above equation becomes x−56=3x6

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 6⋅x−56=6⋅3x6x−5=3xx−x−5=3x−x−5=2x(12)⋅(−5)=(12)⋅(2x)−52=x

We conclude that the solution is x=−52.

Question 14
?

Solve the equation 6x−5=2x.

a
65
b
13
c
−5
d
−52
e
25
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=5 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x−56=x2

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator 6. The above equation becomes x−56=3x6

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 6⋅x−56=6⋅3x6x−5=3xx−x−5=3x−x−5=2x(12)⋅(−5)=(12)⋅(2x)−52=x

We conclude that the solution is x=−52.

question.name: Question 15
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{1}=\frac{5x}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $3.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{6x+3}{3}=\frac{5x}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{6x+3}{3} & =3\cdot \frac{5x}{3} \\ 6x+3 & =5x \\ 6x+3-3 & =5x-3 \\ 6x & =5x-3 \\ 6x-5x & =5x-3-5x \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15

Solve the equation 12x+1=35x.

a
13
b
3
c
−3
d
53
e
−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=−12 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

2x+11=5x3

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator 3. The above equation becomes 6x+33=5x3.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 3⋅6x+33=3⋅5x36x+3=5x6x+3−3=5x−36x=5x−36x−5x=5x−3−5xx=−3

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}

$$

$$

$$

question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=-6$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{1}=\frac{2x+12}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $3.$ We get

$$
\frac{3x+15}{3}=\frac{2x+12}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot (\frac{3x+15}{3}) & =3\cdot (\frac{2x+12}{3}) \\ 3x+15 & =2x+12 \\ 3x-2x & =12-15 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16

Solve the equation 1x+5=32x+12.

a
−2
b
−3
c
3
d
4
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=−5 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=−6 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x+51=2x+123

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, 3. We get

3x+153=2x+123.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 3⋅(3x+153)=3⋅(2x+123)3x+15=2x+123x−2x=12−15x=−3

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=-6$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{1}=\frac{2x+12}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $3.$ We get

$$
\frac{3x+15}{3}=\frac{2x+12}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot (\frac{3x+15}{3}) & =3\cdot (\frac{2x+12}{3}) \\ 3x+15 & =2x+12 \\ 3x-2x & =12-15 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=−12 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=−1 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

2x+15=x+11

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, 5. The equation becomes 2x+15=5x+55.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: (5)⋅2x+15=(5)⋅5x+552x+1=5x+51−5=5x−2x−4=3x(13)⋅(−4)=(13)⋅(3x)(13)⋅(−4)=(13)⋅(3x)−43=x We conclude that the solution is x=−43.

question.name: Question 17
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{x+1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $5.$ The equation becomes

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{5x+5}{5}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5)\cdot \frac{2x+1}{5} & =(5)\cdot \frac{5x+5}{5} \\ 2x+1 & =5x+5 \\ 1-5 & =5x-2x \\ -4 & =3x \\ (\frac{1}{3})\cdot (-4) & =(\frac{1}{3})\cdot (3x) \\ (\frac{1}{3})\cdot (-4) & =(\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) \\ -\frac{4}{3} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{4}{3}.$

question.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations with Binomials in Both Denominators

solution.reasoning: With x\ne3,-6, cross-multiplication gives 6(x+6)=2(x-3), so 4x=-42 and x=-\frac{21}{2}, option d. Substitution makes both sides equal -4/9. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 23 = \dfrac 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 32 = \dfrac x2

question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{x+1} = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac {x+1}{1} = \dfrac 12
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
x+1 = \dfrac 12 .
$$

question.name: Example: Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial and a Monomial in Denominators
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero, and

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{x-2} = \dfrac 3{5x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac {x-2}{1} = \dfrac{5x}{3}
$$

The above equation simplifies to 

$$
x-2 = \dfrac{5x}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot (x-2) & =3\cdot \frac{5x}{3} \\ 3x-6 & =5x \\ 3x-5x & =6 \\ -2x & =6 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Solving Rational Equations with Binomials in Both Denominators
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=\dfrac 12$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero, and

- $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{2x-1} = \dfrac{1}{x+1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{2x-1}{1} = \dfrac{x+1}1
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
2x-1 = x+1.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =x+1 \\ 2x-x & =1+1 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y$ given that $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=4\lambda x \\ -4=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ \lambda y=-2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,y=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies 

$$
\frac{1}{2}y=-2\,⇒\,y=-4.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+(-4)^{2}=4\,⇒\,{x}^{2}=-6\end{aligned}
$$

which has no solutions.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(0,-2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-8$ | $8$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,2),$ and its minimum value is $-8.$

First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving ∇f=0, as follows:

⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨0,0⟩⟨2x,−4⟩=⟨0,0⟩

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Since f(x,y) is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, f(x,y) reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y),g(x,y)=4

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩⟨2x,−4⟩=λ⟨4x,2y⟩

Therefore, we have the following:

{2x=4λx−4=2λy⇒{x(1−2λ)=0λy=−2

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

  • Assuming x=0 in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition g(x,y)=4 implies 2(0)2+y2=4⇒y=±2. This gives the critical points (0,±2).

  • Assuming λ=12 in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies 12y=−2⇒y=−4. Then, the constraint condition g(x,y)=4 implies 2x2+(−4)2=4⇒x2=−6 which has no solutions.

Therefore, f has possible extreme values at the points (0,±2).

We evaluate f at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

(x,y) (0,2) (0,−2)
f(x,y) −8 8

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at (0,2), and its minimum value is −8.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Extreme Values: Cases With No Inner Critical Points
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=4\lambda x \\ -4=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ \lambda y=-2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,y=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies 

$$
\frac{1}{2}y=-2\,⇒\,y=-4.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+(-4)^{2}=4\,⇒\,{x}^{2}=-6\end{aligned}
$$

which has no solutions.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(0,-2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-8$ | $8$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,2),$ and its minimum value is $-8.$

Question 1
?

Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function f(x,y)=x2−4y given that 2x2+y2≤4.

a
4
b
−10
c
1
d
−8
e
−5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving ∇f=0, as follows:

⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨0,0⟩⟨2x,−4⟩=⟨0,0⟩

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of f(x,y) subject to the constraint g(x,y)=2x2+y2=4.

Since f(x,y) is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, f(x,y) reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y),g(x,y)=4

We start by solving the first equation:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩⟨2x,−4⟩=λ⟨4x,2y⟩

Therefore, we have the following:

{2x=4λx−4=2λy⇒{x(1−2λ)=0λy=−2

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

  • Assuming x=0 in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition g(x,y)=4 implies 2(0)2+y2=4⇒y=±2. This gives the critical points (0,±2).

  • Assuming λ=12 in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies 12y=−2⇒y=−4. Then, the constraint condition g(x,y)=4 implies 2x2+(−4)2=4⇒x2=−6 which has no solutions.

Therefore, f has possible extreme values at the points (0,±2).

We evaluate f at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

(x,y) (0,2) (0,−2)
f(x,y) −8 8

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at (0,2), and its minimum value is −8.
question.knowledge_point: Finding Extreme Values: Cases With No Inner Critical Points

solution.reasoning: There are no interior critical points because \nabla f=(2x,-4) never vanishes. On the boundary, Lagrange multipliers give 2x=4\lambda x and -4=2\lambda y. If x\ne0, then \lambda=1/2 and y=-4, which violates the constraint. Thus x=0 and y=\pm2, giving f=-8 and f=8. The minimum is -8 at (0,2), choice d. question.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=x-{y}^{2}$ given that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ -2y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\lambda x=\frac{1}{2} \\ y(1+\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,x=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

- Assuming $\lambda =-1$ in the second equation of the system, the first equation of the system gives 

$$
-x=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 2,0),\,(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).
$$

 

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(-2,0)$ | $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{17}{4}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(2,0),$ and its maximum value is $2.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function f(x,y)=5−x+2y given that 2x2+y2≤4.

a
5−32
b
−42
c
5−423
d
43
e
5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving ∇f=0, as follows:

⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨0,0⟩⟨−1,2⟩=⟨0,0⟩

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of f(x,y) subject to the constraint g(x,y)=2x2+y2=4.

Since f(x,y) is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, f(x,y) reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system: ∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)g(x,y)=4

We start by solving the first equation: ∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y,)⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩⟨−1,2⟩=λ⟨4x,2y⟩

Notice that we cannot have λ=0 since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming λ≠0, we have the following {−1=4λx2=2λy⇒{x=−14λy=1λ⇒x=−14y

Substituting x=−14y into the condition g(x,y)=4, we get 2x2+y2=4y28+y2=4y2=329y=±423

As a result, x=−14y=∓23.

Therefore, f has possible extreme values at the points (−23,423),(23,−423).

We evaluate f at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

(x,y) (−23,423) (23,−423)
f(x,y) 5+32 5−32

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at (23,−423), and its minimum value is 5−32.
question.knowledge_point: Finding Extreme Values: Cases With No Inner Critical Points

solution.reasoning: There are no interior critical points because \nabla f=(-1,2) never vanishes. On the boundary, Lagrange multipliers give -1=4\lambda x and 2=2\lambda y, hence y=-4x. Substitution into 2x^2+y^2=4 gives x=\pm\sqrt{2}/3. The resulting function values are 5\pm3\sqrt{2}, so the minimum is 5-3\sqrt{2}, choice a, attained at (\sqrt{2}/3,-4\sqrt{2}/3). No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was supplied.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=5-x+2y$ given that $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-1=4\lambda x \\ 2=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{1}{4\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{1}{4}y\end{aligned}
$$

 

  Substituting $x=-\frac{1}{4}y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=4,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{32}{9} \\ y & =\pm \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-\frac{1}{4}y=∓\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}),\,(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $5+3\sqrt{2}$ | $5-3\sqrt{2}$ |

 

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})\,,$ and its minimum value is $5-3\sqrt{2}.$

question.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=5-x+2y$ given that $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-1=4\lambda x \\ 2=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{1}{4\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{1}{4}y\end{aligned}
$$

 

  Substituting $x=-\frac{1}{4}y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=4,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{32}{9} \\ y & =\pm \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-\frac{1}{4}y=∓\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}),\,(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}).
$$

| $(x,y)$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |

question.html:
Question 3
?

Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function f(x,y)=5−x+2y given that 2x2+y2≤4.

a
5−32
b
−42
c
5−423
d
43
e
5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving ∇f=0, as follows:

⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨0,0⟩⟨−1,2⟩=⟨0,0⟩

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of f(x,y) subject to the constraint g(x,y)=2x2+y2=4.

Since f(x,y) is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, f(x,y) reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system: ∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)g(x,y)=4

We start by solving the first equation: ∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y,)⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩⟨−1,2⟩=λ⟨4x,2y⟩

Notice that we cannot have λ=0 since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming λ≠0, we have the following {−1=4λx2=2λy⇒{x=−14λy=1λ⇒x=−14y

Substituting x=−14y into the condition g(x,y)=4, we get 2x2+y2=4y28+y2=4y2=329y=±423

As a result, x=−14y=∓23.

Therefore, f has possible extreme values at the points (−23,423),(23,−423).

We evaluate f at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

(x,y) (−23,423) (23,−423)
f(x,y) 5+32 5−32

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at (23,−423), and its minimum value is 5−32.

question.name: Example: Finding Extreme Values: Cases With No Inner Critical Points
question.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + y$ given that $2x^2 + 3y^2 \leq 1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= 2x^2 + 3y^2  = 1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,6y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=4\lambda x \\ 1=6\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ \lambda y=\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  = 1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)^{2}+3{y}^{2}=1\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \right).$

- Assuming $\lambda = \dfrac12$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system gives 

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}y = \dfrac{1}{6} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad y = \dfrac1{3}.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  =1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+3{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}=1\,⇒\,x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
\left(0,\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \right), \qquad  \left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right).
$$

 

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $\left(0, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$ | $\left(0, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$ | $\left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ | $-\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ | $\dfrac{2}{3}$ |

 

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $\left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right),$ and its maximum value is $\dfrac23.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-12y=14x{e}^{-4x}
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{-4x}+B{e}^{3x}+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constants omitted):*

$$
\int x{e}^{-7x}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{49}(7x+1){e}^{-7x}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the following differential equation. y″+y′−12y=14xe−4x The general solution to this equation can be written as y(x)=Ae−4x+Be3x+g(x), where A and B are constants. Which of the following could be the function g(x)?

Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constants omitted): ∫xe−7xdx=−149(7x+1)e−7x

a
 −(x2+3x7)e−4x
b
 −(x2+2x5)e−4x
c
−(x2+2x7)e−4x
d
 −(x2+x3)e−4x
e
 −(x2+x7)e−4x
Submit

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-12y=14x{e}^{-4x}
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{-4x}+B{e}^{3x}+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constants omitted):*

$$
\int x{e}^{-7x}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{49}(7x+1){e}^{-7x}
$$

solution.reasoning: With y_1=e^{-4x} and y_2=e^{3x}, the Wronskian is 7e^{-x}. Variation of parameters gives u_1=-∫2x dx=-x² and u_2=∫2xe^{-7x} dx=-(2/49)(7x+1)e^{-7x}. Thus a particular solution is -(x²+2x/7+2/49)e^{-4x}. Absorbing the homogeneous term -(2/49)e^{-4x} into Ae^{-4x} gives option c. Direct substitution verifies that this choice yields 14xe^{-4x}; option a instead yields (14x+1)e^{-4x}. Question 1
?

Consider the following differential equation. y″+y′−12y=14xe−4x The general solution to this equation can be written as y(x)=Ae−4x+Be3x+g(x), where A and B are constants. Which of the following could be the function g(x)?

Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result (integration constants omitted): ∫xe−7xdx=−149(7x+1)e−7x

a
 −(x2+3x7)e−4x
b
 −(x2+2x5)e−4x
c
−(x2+2x7)e−4x
d
 −(x2+x3)e−4x
e
 −(x2+x7)e−4x

question.name: Example: Solving a Differential Equation Whose Characteristic Equation Has Real Roots
question.problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
y'' - 2y' + y = 18x e^{x}
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x) = A e^{x} + B x e^{x} + g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. What could be the function $g(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$. Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution $y_p$ may be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where $u_1$ and $u_2$ satisfy the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
u_1(x) = -\int \dfrac{f(x)y_2(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,dx,
\qquad
u_2(x) = \int \dfrac{f(x)y_1(x)}{W(y_1,y_2)}\,dx,
$$

where $W(y_1,y_2)$ is the Wronskian.

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c(x) = A e^{x} + B x e^{x}.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
y_1(x) = e^{x}, \qquad y_2(x) = x e^{x}.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{x})(x{e}^{x})^{′}-({e}^{x})^{′}(x{e}^{x}) \\  & =({e}^{x})({e}^{x}+x{e}^{x})-({e}^{x})(x{e}^{x}) \\  & ={e}^{2x}+x{e}^{2x}-x{e}^{2x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are independent.

Now compute $u_1(x)$ and $u_2(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{18x{e}^{x}\cdot x{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =-18\int {x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-6{x}^{3} \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{18x{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =18\int x\,dx \\  & =9{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(-6{x}^{3}){e}^{x}+(9{x}^{2})(x{e}^{x}) \\  & =-6{x}^{3}{e}^{x}+9{x}^{3}{e}^{x} \\  & =3{x}^{3}{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}+{{3{x}^{3}{e}^{x}}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x) = 3x^3 e^{x}.
$$
